summary: ModBondDepository is an Olympus-style bond desk: it holds a pre-funded balance of the payout token (fund() is permissionless and one-way), sells it at a debt-dependent discount to the wired oracle's price, forwards the quote payment straight to the treasury sink (or the owner when none is wired), and vests the buyer's payout linearly over vestingTerm with one open bond per address. The mechanics that are there are sound: redeem() is always solvent because deposit() checks the reserve up front and nothing else can remove payout tokens, the linear vest and claimed accounting are correct, and state is updated before the payout transfer. The worst problem is pricing: the bond is priced off a single instantaneous oracle read with no TWAP, no deviation band, no per-bond default cap (maxBondSize starts at uint256.max) and no per-epoch cap, and the debt ceiling is checked before the new payout is added, so with the AMM spot oracle the docs tell deployers to use, one flash-loan-assisted transaction can buy the entire funded reserve for dust; vesting only delays delivery, and the proceeds are already in the treasury. Independently, payoutFor() assumes both tokens share decimals, so an 18-decimal token sold for USDC pays buyers 10^-12 of what they bought (with no refund path), while the reverse pairing lets anyone drain the reserve. The owner can also re-point the oracle and zero the vesting term instantly, which turns any donated reserve into the owner's. Not safe to deploy as-is with a spot oracle or mismatched-decimal tokens; usable behind a TWAP/signed feed, same-decimals tokens (or an oracle pre-scaled for the difference), finite maxBondSize, and a timelocked owner.

findings.title: Spot oracle read with no size, epoch or post-deposit debt bound: one manipulated block buys the entire funded payout reserve
findings.where: bondPrice() L72-L79, payoutFor() L81-L85, deposit() L89-L117 (checks L94-L100); composed with ModAMM.price() amm.sol L108-L111
findings.detail: deposit() prices the whole bond off a single live oracle.price() read and the only quantity bounds are maxBondSize (defaults to type(uint256).max, L60) and the payout balance held by the depository (L96-L99). The catalog docs and the header comment (L11-L12) tell the deployer to point the oracle port at the AMM pair the token trades on; ModAMM.price() is the raw spot ratio reserve1*1e18/reserve0 with no TWAP, so it moves within one transaction. Vesting does not protect the protocol: it delays delivery of the payout tokens, it does not reduce how many were sold or at what price, and the quote proceeds are already forwarded to the treasury (L106) with no clawback. The catalog also ships ModFlashLender and a ModFixedOracle whose owner can set any price (see oracle.json ORACLE-1), so both a permissionless and a key-holder version of this path exist on the same canvas. There is no per-block or per-epoch sales cap and the debt ceiling is checked before the new payout is added (BONDING-3), so nothing between the manipulated price and the reserve limits the damage.
findings.exploit: Canvas: token PT (payout), USDC-like quote Q, ModAMM(PT,Q) with reserves 1,000,000 PT / 1,000,000 Q (price 1e18), ModBondDepository(oracle = amm, discount 700), depository funded with 500,000 PT via fund(). Attacker holds or flash-borrows 9,000,000 PT (ModFlashLender on PT, or a large holder) and in ONE transaction: (1) amm.swap(PT->Q, 9,000,000) - reserves become 10,000,000 PT / ~100,000 Q, amm.price() = 0.01e18; (2) bonding.deposit(quoteAmount = 5,000 Q, maxPrice = 0.01e18): bondPrice = 0.0093e18, payoutFor = 5,000e18*1e18/0.0093e18 = 537,000 PT, capped only by the INSUFFICIENT_PAYOUT_RESERVE check, so attacker sizes quoteAmount to take all 500,000 PT for ~4,650 Q; (3) amm.swap(Q->PT) to restore the pool and repay the flash loan, paying only the round-trip AMM fee. The protocol sold 500,000 PT for 4,650 Q instead of ~465,000 Q; the tokens vest over 5 days and are then redeemed. Same outcome with ModFixedOracle if its owner is not the depository's owner: oracle.setPrice(1) then deposit(1 wei).
findings.recommendation: Never price a bond off an instantaneous spot read: consume a TWAP (time-weighted over many blocks) or a signed/Chainlink feed, and add an on-contract sanity band (revert if oracle.price() deviates more than X% from the last accepted bond price). Bound the damage of any single read: set a real maxBondSize, add a per-epoch sales cap (e.g. maxPayoutPerEpoch with a rolling window like Olympus's `maxPayout` as bps of supply), and make the debt ceiling bind on totalDebt + payout (BONDING-3). Keep the depository stocked with only what it intends to sell in the near term rather than the whole allocation.

findings.title: payoutFor() assumes payout and quote tokens share decimals; a 6/18-decimal pair mis-prices by 10^12 (reserve drained, or buyers robbed)
findings.where: payoutFor() L81-L85; bondPrice() L72-L79; IOracle common.sol L20-L23
findings.detail: payout = quoteAmount * 1e18 / price treats `price` as quote RAW units per payout RAW unit x1e18. That equals the documented IOracle unit ('price of one whole token, scaled 1e18') only when quoteToken.decimals() == payoutToken.decimals(). Neither the constructor nor deposit() reads decimals() from either token, and the catalog exposes no hint. ModAMM.price() happens to return the raw ratio so it is implicitly correct; ModFixedOracle (and any Chainlink-style adapter returning the human price) is not. If the payout token has FEWER decimals than the quote token, payouts are inflated by 10^(quoteDec-payoutDec) and anyone can empty the depository's payout balance for dust. If it has MORE decimals (the common case: 18-dec protocol token sold for USDC), payouts are deflated by the same factor and every buyer pays full price for 10^-12 of the tokens; the proceeds have already gone to the treasury (L106) and there is no refund path, so this is a direct loss to users, not a revert.
findings.exploit: Case A (reserve drain): payoutToken = 6-dec token PT, quoteToken = 18-dec DAI, ModFixedOracle initialPrice = 1e18 ('1 DAI per PT'), depository funded with 1,000,000 PT (1e12 raw). Attacker calls deposit(1e12 /*0.000001 DAI*/, 1e18): payout = 1e12*1e18/(0.93e18) = ~1.075e12 raw = 1,075,000 PT; the reserve check clamps only if smaller, so the attacker takes the entire 1,000,000 PT reserve for 0.000001 DAI, vests 5 days, redeems. Case B (buyer loss): payoutToken 18-dec PT, quoteToken USDC (6-dec), price 1e18. A user deposits 1,000 USDC = 1e9 raw: payout = 1e9*1e18/0.93e18 = 1.075e9 raw = 0.000000001 PT. The 1,000 USDC is already in the treasury.
findings.recommendation: Normalise explicitly: read both decimals() in the constructor and compute payout = quoteAmount * 10**payoutDecimals * 1e18 / (price * 10**quoteDecimals), so `price` can honestly be the whole-token price the IOracle interface promises. Until then, document on the catalog param that the oracle must return quote-raw per payout-raw x1e18, and have the composer pre-scale ModFixedOracle's initialPrice by 10^(quoteDec-payoutDec) when it wires this block, exactly as oracle.json ORACLE-4 recommends for lending/cdp.

findings.title: Debt ceiling is checked before the new payout is added and the discount is taken at pre-deposit debt, so one bond can jump straight to (and past) the ceiling at the maximum discount
findings.where: deposit() L91-L100 (bondPrice at L91, DEBT_CEILING at L100); debtRatioBps() L64-L68; constructor default maxBondSize L60
findings.detail: The header sells the debt ratio as 'the control loop that stops a bond from selling the whole treasury into one dip' (L12-L14), but the loop never sees the bond being bought. L100 requires debtRatioBps() < maxDebtBps using totalDebt BEFORE `payout` is added (L114), and L91 prices the whole bond at that same pre-deposit ratio. With maxBondSize defaulting to unlimited, a single deposit at ratio 0 gets the full discountBps on every token, and can push totalDebt to 100% of supply in one call; the ceiling then blocks only the NEXT buyer. The intended behaviour (discount shrinking as debt fills, ceiling binding on the marginal token) is therefore unenforced, and the economic leak is the full discount on the entire reserve rather than the average along the curve. Splitting into many small bonds is not even needed - it is the opposite: one large bond is strictly better for the buyer than many small ones.
findings.exploit: payoutToken supply 10,000,000, maxDebtBps 2,000 (ceiling = 2,000,000 debt), depository funded with 5,000,000 PT, discount 700. totalDebt = 0. Buyer calls deposit(quote for 5,000,000 PT at market): L91 bondPrice = market * 0.93 (ratio 0 -> full discount), L100 passes (0 < 2000), L114 sets totalDebt = 5,000,000 = 50% of supply, 2.5x the ceiling. Every token was sold at the deepest discount. Combined with BONDING-1 the same call is what lets a manipulated price take the whole reserve.
findings.recommendation: Bind the ceiling on the post-deposit state: require((totalDebt + payout) * 10_000 / supply <= maxDebtBps). Cap each bond as bps of supply (Olympus maxPayout) and default maxBondSize to something finite, e.g. 1% of payoutToken.totalSupply(). Optionally price large bonds along the curve (integrate the discount over [ratioBefore, ratioAfter]) so a large buyer does not get the zero-debt discount on every token.

findings.title: Owner can drain a reserve that anyone may have donated: setOracle/setTerms/setTreasury are instant, unbounded and undelayed while fund() is permissionless and one-way
findings.where: fund() L141-L143; setOracle() L149-L152; setTerms() L154-L165; setTreasury() L145-L147; deposit() L105-L106
findings.detail: fund() lets any address push payout tokens into the depository (typical composition: a DAO treasury or the token's mint authority stocks a depository operated by a separate key), and nothing lets a funder take them back. The owner, however, can (a) setOracle to a ModFixedOracle they control at price 1 and deposit(1 wei) to be owed the entire reserve; (b) setTerms(discount, vestingTerm = 0, maxDebtBps = 0, maxBondSize = max), which turns the depository into an instant swap with no ceiling; (c) setTreasury to their own EOA, or leave it unset so proceeds default to `owner` (L105). None of these has a delay, a two-step, or an event, and the catalog's ctor makes the deployer EOA the owner unless the governor port is wired. So whoever holds the owner key holds every token ever funded plus all future bond proceeds. Note the only legitimate way to recover unsold tokens is this same rigged-oracle path (BONDING-8), which encourages operators to hold exactly this power.
findings.exploit: DAO calls fund(2,000,000 PT) into a depository whose owner is the deployer EOA. Owner: (1) deploy ModFixedOracle(price = 1); (2) bonding.setOracle(thatOracle); (3) bonding.setTerms(0, 0, 0, type(uint256).max); (4) bonding.deposit(2,000,000 /* 2e-12 quote */, 1) - bondPrice = 1, payoutFor = 2,000,000e18 * 1e18 / 1 clamped by the reserve check to the full 2,000,000 PT, vestingTerm 0 so vested() returns everything immediately; (5) redeem(). The DAO's donation is gone in four owner transactions and one 2-wei deposit.
findings.recommendation: Wire the governor port to ModTimelock/ModGovernor for any depository that holds third-party funds, and emit events on every setter so watchers can react inside the delay. Harden the setters: setOracle should require the new feed's price to be within a band of the old one; setTerms should enforce a minimum vestingTerm and a finite maxBondSize; setTreasury should reject address(0). Add a permissioned withdrawSurplus (BONDING-8) so operators do not need oracle-rigging as their exit.

findings.title: maxPrice guards only the price; a setTerms() landing ahead of a deposit can change the vesting term the buyer is committing to
findings.detail: The buyer's only slippage argument is maxPrice. vestingTerm is read at L112 at inclusion time, so a setTerms transaction mined between simulation and inclusion (owner action, or an owner tx already in the mempool) silently changes the bond the user gets: a 5-day vest becomes a 5-year vest with the same payout and the quote already forwarded to the treasury. Discount changes are covered by maxPrice, and a lowered maxBondSize just reverts, so the term is the one parameter the buyer cannot defend.
findings.exploit: Owner broadcasts setTerms(700, 157_680_000 /* 5 years */, 2000, max). A user who simulated a 5-day bond has deposit(quote, maxPrice) pending. Ordering: setTerms, then deposit. deposit passes (price unchanged), writes end = now + 5 years. The user's quote is in the treasury and their payout is locked for five years; redeem() releases 1/1826 of it per day.
findings.recommendation: Add an expected-term (or maxVestingTerm) argument to deposit() and revert on mismatch, mirroring maxPrice; a minPayout argument is also worth adding so decimal or ceiling changes cannot silently shrink the bond.

findings.title: Treasury fallback routes reserves to `owner`, which can be address(0) after setOwner(0); ModToken then burns every payment, other tokens brick deposits
findings.where: deposit() L105-L106; setTreasury() L145-L147; Owned.setOwner common.sol L47-L50; ERC20Base._move common.sol L93-L100
findings.detail: When treasury is unset (or explicitly set to address(0)) proceeds are pushed to `owner`. Owned.setOwner accepts address(0), a common 'renounce' move once a protocol wants to look immutable. After that every bond's quote payment is transferred to address(0): ERC20Base (ModToken, ModAMM LP, etc.) has no zero-address check in _move, so the tokens are silently burned and totalSupply never decreases; OpenZeppelin-style tokens revert, so deposit() is bricked with no way to fix it (setTreasury needs the owner that no longer exists). Separately, a deployer who leaves the treasury port unwired sends real protocol revenue to an EOA rather than a sink, which is probably not what the canvas intended.
findings.exploit: Deployer wires no treasury, launches, then calls setOwner(address(0)) to 'renounce'. Next deposit(1000 Q, maxPrice): L105 to = address(0); L106 pushes 1000 Q to address(0). If Q is a ModToken the transfer succeeds and the 1000 Q are gone forever while the buyer still receives a vesting bond; every subsequent bond does the same. If Q is USDC the push reverts and the depository is permanently dead.
findings.recommendation: require(treasury_ != address(0)) in setTreasury and require a non-zero treasury in the constructor (make the treasury port required, or default it to the owner at deploy and revert if owner is zero); reject address(0) in Owned.setOwner or use a two-step transfer. Emit a TreasuryChanged event.

findings.title: Non-standard quote tokens: fee-on-transfer bricks deposit(), and a hook token lets a reentrant deposit permanently inflate totalDebt
findings.where: deposit() L102-L115 (pull L102, push L106, bond write L108, totalDebt L114); BOND_OPEN check L95
findings.detail: deposit pulls quoteAmount and immediately pushes the same quoteAmount onward; a fee-on-transfer quote token leaves the contract short so the push reverts (PUSH_FAILED) - every deposit fails, and any quote dust someone sent to the contract is slowly drained to cover fees. With an ERC777/hook quote token the state writes happen after the external calls: a reentrant deposit() from the transfer hook passes the BOND_OPEN check (L95, the outer bond is not written yet) and the reserve check (L96-L99, totalDebt not yet incremented), writes bonds[attacker] and adds payout2 to totalDebt; the outer call then overwrites bonds[attacker] with payout1 and adds payout1 too. payout2 is now counted in totalDebt forever because no bond can ever redeem it. The attacker pays for both bonds (proceeds reach the treasury), so this is griefing at cost, but the phantom debt raises debtRatioBps() for everyone, shrinking the discount and, with enough of it, tripping DEBT_CEILING for all future buyers with no admin function to correct totalDebt.
findings.exploit: quoteToken is an ERC777. Attacker contract calls deposit(q1, max); inside its tokensToSend hook during the pull at L102 it calls deposit(q2, max) again, which completes fully (bond = payout2, totalDebt += payout2). Control returns, L108 overwrites bond = payout1, L114 totalDebt += payout1. Attacker redeems payout1 over the term; payout2 never leaves totalDebt. Repeat until debtRatioBps() >= maxDebtBps: deposit() now reverts DEBT_CEILING for every user, permanently.
findings.recommendation: Write the bond and totalDebt before the external token calls (CEI), or add a nonReentrant guard; measure received amount as balanceAfter - balanceBefore and forward that. Document that fee-on-transfer and hook tokens are unsupported on the quote port, and add an owner-only `syncDebt()` that recomputes totalDebt from an enumerable set of open bonds or at least a guarded manual correction.

findings.title: No way to withdraw unsold payout tokens: fund() is one-way, so the only exit is the oracle-rigging path in BONDING-4
findings.where: fund() L141-L143; absence of any withdraw function
findings.detail: Solvency is good - redeem() is always backed because the reserve check at L96-L99 runs at deposit time and nothing can remove payout tokens except redeem() - but the flip side is that a depository that is wound down, re-priced, or simply over-stocked cannot return its surplus. A well-behaved operator has to either leave tokens stranded or perform exactly the setOracle-to-dust trick that BONDING-4 warns about, which trains users to accept that behaviour from operators.
findings.exploit: n/a - operational limitation. Operator funds 1,000,000 PT, sells 100,000, decides to stop bonding: 900,000 PT are locked unless the owner rigs the oracle and 'buys' them for dust.
findings.recommendation: Add withdrawSurplus(address to, uint256 amount) onlyOwner with require(payoutToken.balanceOf(address(this)) - amount >= totalDebt), emit an event, and route it through the timelock like other setters. This keeps every open bond fully backed while giving operators a clean exit.

findings.title: One bond per address, and maxDebtBps = 0 means 'no ceiling' in deposit() but 'no discount' in bondPrice()
findings.where: BOND_OPEN check L95; bonds mapping L38; bondPrice() L75-L77 vs deposit() L100
findings.detail: An address cannot open a second bond until its first is fully vested AND fully redeemed (payout == claimed), so a wallet is locked out for the whole vestingTerm after each purchase, and any contract that bonds on behalf of many users (a router, a zap, a vault strategy) can hold only one position for the entire protocol. Not a fund-loss issue (bonds are keyed by msg.sender, nobody else can overwrite them), but it silently caps throughput and breaks the common integration pattern. Separately, setTerms(…, maxDebtBps_ = 0, …) is a foot-gun: bondPrice() treats 0 as 'discount is zero' while deposit() treats it as 'no ceiling', so the flag means unlimited full-price bonding, which is unlikely to be what anyone wants. The linear vest itself (vested() L119-L126) is correct: elapsed/(end-start) with claimed tracked, full remainder at or after end, and vestingTerm = 0 vests instantly without a division by zero.
findings.exploit: n/a - a vault strategy bonds 100 PT for its depositors; every further bond from that strategy reverts BOND_OPEN for the full vesting term.
findings.recommendation: Key bonds by (address, index) or an incrementing bondId with per-bond redeem, as Olympus v2 does. Reject maxDebtBps_ == 0 in setTerms (or give it one meaning) and document the semantics on the catalog param.

safe_use: Do not wire the oracle port to ModAMM.price() (raw spot) or to a ModFixedOracle owned by anyone other than the depository's governor. Use a TWAP or signed feed, and keep the depository stocked with only what you intend to sell in the near term - the funded balance is the loss ceiling for a bad price.

Use payout and quote tokens with the SAME decimals, or pre-scale the oracle: the contract needs quote-raw per payout-raw x1e18, i.e. humanPrice * 10^(quoteDecimals - payoutDecimals) * 1e18. Simulate payoutFor(1 whole quote token) before the first real bond and check it returns the expected number of raw payout units.

Immediately after deploy call setTerms with a finite maxBondSize (e.g. 0.5-1% of payout supply) and keep maxDebtBps > 0; the constructor default allows one buyer to take everything at the full discount.

Wire the treasury port (feesplitter or treasury block) - unwired, every bond payment goes to the owner EOA - and never call setOwner(address(0)) on this block; with no treasury that burns or bricks every payment.

Wire the governor port to ModTimelock or ModGovernor if anyone other than the owner funds the depository: setOracle, setTerms and setTreasury are instant and together let the owner take the whole reserve and all proceeds.
Quote token must be a plain ERC20: no fee-on-transfer (deposits revert) and no transfer hooks (reentrant deposits can permanently inflate totalDebt and trip the debt ceiling for everyone).
Tell buyers to pass a tight maxPrice and to redeem() fully before bonding again; one open bond per address, and a setTerms in flight can change the vesting term they receive.
